note:
Both halves landed and measured.

Q4_K: dequantQ4_KInto reslices to fixed lengths (raw[o:o+q4kBlockSize], dst[base:base+64]) instead of the open-ended form. MEASURED 177,736 -> 154,195 ns on BenchmarkDequantQ4_K, 1.15x. The per-element IsInBounds at q4k.go:75:8 and :76:8 are gone, replaced by one IsSliceInBounds per sub-block — N per-element checks traded for one per-run check. Bit-identity structural: no arithmetic expression changed, y[l] addresses the same element as dst[base+l] by construction.

Q6_K: the four scale products were recomputed on every one of 32 iterations to produce 8 distinct values per 128-element group, because is := l / 16 takes only two values. Split the loop at that boundary and hoisted them, plus the same fixed-length reslicing. MEASURED 230,684 -> 178,457 ns on BenchmarkDequantQ6_K, 1.29x, and IsInBounds in the loop body drops to zero.

BIT-IDENTITY, the part that mattered: Q6_K touches arithmetic GROUPING, so the structural argument used for Q4_K does not carry. The original d * float32(int8(sc[...])) * float32(q-32) associates left-to-right as (d*sc)*(q-32); hoisting s := d*sc and writing s*(q-32) reproduces that grouping exactly, whereas folding the other way as d*(sc*(q-32)) would not. That argument was VERIFIED rather than trusted: the raw output bits were captured for a deterministic 7-block input before and after (7,168 bytes) and compared byte-for-byte — identical. The capture harness was removed afterwards; the existing golden, round-trip, hostile-input and fuzz suites remain the standing gates and all pass.

Both A/Bs used an interleaved three-round file-copy toggle on the same host in one session, medians reported — after an earlier non-interleaved comparison on a different task was shown to be unreliable by a control benchmark that moved 20 percent with no code change.

CORRECTION carried forward from the original brief: it claimed q5k.go and q2k.go compile bounds-check-free and could serve as the clean comparison. They do NOT — a check_bce dump reports 29 findings across those two files. Their idiom is still the right model for the inner store loop, but the blanket claim is wrong.

NOT DONE, deliberately: the NEON/SIMD dequant kernels the brief listed as a follow-on. Both fixes here are the correct precursor — with the scales hoisted the Q6_K inner loop is a pure vmul over 16 lanes — but the vectorization itself is a separate, larger change needing its own arch-gated parity work, and it belongs with the arm64 SIMD tasks rather than here. No perfscan rule was minted for this pattern: the loop-invariant-per-stride shape is already specified in the reduce/odometer detector task, and duplicating it here would create two rules for one anti-pattern.

THE TASK'S CAUTION WAS RIGHT TO DEMAND A MEASUREMENT AND WRONG ABOUT THE DIRECTION. It argued the aggressive quants might not repay fusion the way the deployment formats did, because they do more per-element unpacking. They repaid it MORE (1.41-1.75x against 1.40-1.52x). The alloc signature the task said to check first — 107 vs 102 per decode step — was present on all three and was the correct predictor; the reasoning about unpacking cost was not.

PS6003 FALSE-POSITIVED ON THE FIRST DRAFT AND THE CODE WAS CHANGED, NOT THE RULE. Wrapping a dispatch switch in a single `if m == 1` guard hides the covered set behind a function value the AST check cannot follow, so it reported a gap that no longer existed. Naming the five types in the guard keeps coverage legible to the check and meaningful for whoever adds an eighth type. Teaching the rule dataflow would have cost soundness and bought nothing. body:
Two of the three gguf candidates that the previous rounds synthetic benchmark unblocked.

(1) The data section is now sized from the tensor table rather than grown by io.ReadAll, which reallocates at about 1.25x and copies on every growth. The size is derived from bytes the parser has already read — no Stat, no seekable reader. BenchmarkReadFileSynth/tensor-heavy -17.7 percent time and -14.3 percent bytes; header-heavy unchanged within noise (a first single-order round read +4.2 percent, the reverse order put the presized version slightly ahead, so the honest report is no change — its data section is a few hundred KB).

THE TABLE IS UNTRUSTED INPUT AND THE FIRST DRAFT FORGOT IT: TestHostileTensorOffsetOverflow caught an offset near 2^64 wrapping the addition and panicking in makeslice. Two guards now, the subtraction form for the overflow and a 1 TiB bound on any DECLARED size above which the old discovery path runs, allocating only what the file holds. A parser must not let a file claim about its own size decide how much memory to allocate. The error path changed and is pinned: a file whose table promises more than it holds now fails at the parse naming the shortfall, which is strictly better than the later per-tensor range error.

(2) The Q6_K dequant inner loop wrote four elements per iteration at constant strides, each with its own bounds check. One fixed-length window cut them to a single slice check per 128-element group: BenchmarkDequantQ6_K -16.5 percent, confirmed with the compilers BCE diagnostic. It was the LAST of its family — both sibling dequants and the same files own dot-product already had the window.

CHECK ADDED: PS3030 fixed-offset-stores-not-windowed, deliberately separate from PS3019 (unrolled lanes under a len bound, where the obstacle is integer overflow on i+K) because the premise differs even though the remedy matches. 2 findings pre-fix, 0 after, 1 advisory candidate in the same files encoder.

NOT TAKEN: claiming tensors largest-first instead of in file order. The synthetic benchmark builds uniform tensors, so an LPT schedule cannot show anything on it; measuring that needs a benchmark with a deliberately skewed size distribution, which is the next piece of instrumentation rather than a code change. Also still open: the Quantize input copy for contiguous F32, ref SolveSPD, and the ReadRaw per-tensor copy which has no benchmark.

body:
SHIPPED. ReadRaw copied every tensor out of the parse buffer — a full model-size allocation and memmove on every quantized load. Tensors are now three-index slices of that buffer. BenchmarkReadRawSynth 1002129 to 466473 ns/op (-53.5 percent) and 18950344 to 9513152 B/op (-49.8 percent).

THE BENCHMARK CAME FIRST AND WAS THE UNBLOCK, again: ReadRaw is what a caller uses to load a model WITHOUT materializing full-precision weights, so its cost is the one quantized inference pays, and it had no instrumentation at all because Read dequantization dominates the other path and hid it.

CONTRACT CHANGE, documented on the function: QuantTensor.Data is a READ-ONLY VIEW into one shared buffer. Writing through one tensor corrupts its neighbors and retaining any tensor retains the whole data section. For the ordinary whole-model case this is strictly LESS memory than before, because the per-tensor copies sat on top of the buffer they came from; a caller keeping one tensor and dropping the rest must copy the slice. The capacity clamp is load-bearing rather than decorative — without it an append to one tensor overwrites the next one bytes in place — and the gate checks cap equals len, reddening when the clamp is removed.

MEASURED AND NOT TAKEN: one shared slab with the copies kept. -2.4 percent, within noise: 64 tensors means 64 allocations saved out of 4282 and the copies are the actual cost. Recorded so the cheaper-looking option is not retried.

PROCESS: the aliasing was raised as a decision because it changes a public contract. The answer was a STANDING INSTRUCTION to stop asking and always take the measured optimization, now rule NEVER-ASK-TAKE-THE-MEASURED-WIN-001. Future contract-changing optimizations are implemented and documented rather than escalated.

STILL OPEN: gguf largest-first tensor claiming (needs a skewed-size benchmark), and a sound version of the invariant-inner-loop check withheld last round.

body:
The gguf decode cursor claims tensors in FILE order, and a GGUF writer emits them in name order, so an embedding or output matrix that dwarfs every per-block weight is routinely claimed LAST — picked up when the fewest workers remain to overlap it. Longest-Processing-Time-first bounds the makespan at 4/3 minus 1/(3m) of optimal where file order has no bound at all. It has been on the candidate list for several rounds and looked like a clear win.

IT IS NOT A WIN ON THIS SYSTEM. Implemented (sort a claim-order permutation by descending byte size, results still landing in decoded[i] by original index) and measured at two skews: 48 small plus 3 big gave +0.3 percent, and 11 small plus 1 huge gave -2.2 percent, inside the spread. Reverted.

WHY THE ARGUMENT FAILED: it is correct about scheduling and wrong about what dominates. The decode is bandwidth-bound and twelve workers already overlap most of the tail, so the imbalance one large tensor creates is a small fraction of the makespan. A bound on the makespan only matters when the makespan is set by imbalance rather than by bandwidth.

THE BENCHMARK STAYS, with the null result in its doc comment. BenchmarkReadFileSkewed is the only cell that can see a scheduling change at all — BenchmarkReadFileSynth builds UNIFORM tensors, so every claim order produces the same makespan there, which is exactly why this idea sat unmeasured for so long. Anyone reaching for it again finds the measurement rather than the intuition.

STILL OPEN: a sound version of the invariant-inner-loop check withheld two rounds ago, whose diagnosis is recorded (invariance must be tested against EVERY enclosing index and against variables assigned in enclosing bodies, plus a suppression for loops already at the hoisted position).
gist: No action on the transform: largest-first claiming measured +0.3 percent and -2.2 percent at two skews, both inside the spread, and was reverted — the decode is bandwidth-bound so a makespan bound improves a quantity that does not dominate. The BenchmarkReadFileSkewed cell ships and carries the null result in its doc comment, since it is the only cell that can see a scheduling change at all.

note: Authorized by the approved parent T-01KYJNDV2VFRFR5RDBSPKJBRVK and the standing M2-first performance mandate. Tier A presizing and ReadRaw views already shipped; this slice isolates tier B mmap for ReadFile with a measured TinyLlama baseline.

DONE: ReadFile maps supported regular files read-only, parses the encoded data section in place, waits for parallel readParsed materialization, then unmaps before return. Unsupported platforms, mapping failures, empty files, and non-regular files retain the buffered path; concurrent truncation is documented outside the contract.

MEASURED on Apple M2 Pro with a real 638 MiB TinyLlama-1.1B Q4_K_M file, ten fresh-process order-alternating pairs: 182.00 ms buffered versus 97.12 ms mmap, 1.87x faster (-46.64%, p=0.000, n=10). Heap bytes fell from 4.735 GiB/op to 4.113 GiB/op (-13.14%, about 668 MB/op); allocations were unchanged. On the matched deterministic 64 MiB F32 full-materialization fixture, six alternating sessions measured GoAI 3.04 ms versus gguf-py 0.19.0 at 6.22 ms: GoAI 2.05x ahead.

CORRECTNESS: mapped output is exact against the buffered control across all metadata and tensor values after the mapping has been released. Both parsers reject a truncated data section. Package tests, race detector, Windows fallback cross-compile, go vet, typed Spectackle graph, and repository preflight pass. Evidence is under internal/benchcompare/leadership/evidence/m2-gguf-readfile-mmap-20260817. Landed implementation commit: 273e894a.

CONTRACT: GGUF-READFILE-MMAP-LIFETIME-001. Generalizable staging pattern: jxsl13/perfscan#754.

DELIBERATELY NOT DONE: mmap for ReadRaw. RawFile returns views into its parse buffer; mapping it without a new explicit lifetime/Close contract would expose unmapped slices or silently retain mappings. That is a separate API-design task.
